Draft better messages with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), find tone-ready examples among [writing prompts](/prompts/category/writing), or polish application letters using the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder).

faq.q: How do I make AI writing sound like me?
faq.a: Paste a short sample you wrote, ask the AI to describe your style, correct that description, then request new text in that style. Add your own facts and edit the result so it reflects your voice.

faq.q: What are good tone words to use in prompts?
faq.a: Pair two or three qualities, such as warm and direct, calm and reassuring, or confident but humble. Combining qualities avoids extremes and gives the AI a clearer picture than a single word like professional.

faq.q: Why does AI writing sound robotic?
faq.a: Models default to a neutral, polished style with generic phrases. Counter this by naming the audience, setting concrete style rules, banning cliches, giving a sample, and adding your own specific details.

faq.q: Can I ask AI to copy a famous author's style?
faq.a: You can ask for general stylistic qualities, but avoid reproducing an author's actual text or presenting imitation as your own work. Use your own writing samples and keep the final work original.

title: System Prompts and Custom Instructions: What They Are
excerpt: System prompts and custom instructions set standing rules for how AI behaves. Learn the difference, what to include, and templates you can adapt for yourself.
seo_title: System Prompts and Custom Instructions: What They Are
seo_description: Understand system prompts and custom instructions: what they do, how they differ from normal prompts, what to include, plus templates and mistakes to avoid.
content:
A system prompt is a set of standing instructions that tells an AI how to behave across a whole conversation, such as its role, tone and rules. Custom instructions are the everyday, user-facing version of the same idea: preferences you save once so you do not have to repeat them in every message.

Understanding both helps you stop retyping the same background and get consistent answers.

## System prompt vs. user prompt

Think of two layers:

- **System-level instructions** set the stage: who the assistant is, what it should always or never do, how it should format answers.
- **User messages** are the individual requests you send during the chat.

When you use an AI product, the company or developer may already have written a system prompt you cannot see. When you build your own assistant, write a custom GPT-style persona, or use a settings page for personal preferences, you can add your own standing layer. Features and names vary between tools, so check the official help pages of the product you use for exactly what is available.

## What custom instructions are good for

Standing instructions are useful for things that stay true across tasks:

- your role or background ("I am a secondary-school science teacher")
- your preferred reading level and language
- formatting habits ("use short paragraphs and bullet points")
- tone preferences ("direct and friendly, no flattery")
- behaviours you want ("ask a clarifying question if my request is ambiguous")
- limits ("do not invent sources; say when you are unsure")

They are not good for details that change with each task, such as the specific essay you are editing today. Put those in the normal prompt.

## Anatomy of a good set of instructions

A compact structure works well:

1. **Who I am and what I use this for.**
2. **How I want answers to look.**
3. **Rules about honesty and uncertainty.**
4. **What to do when information is missing.**

### Template: personal assistant

```
About me: I am a [role/student level] who uses AI for [main purposes].

How to answer:
- Start with the direct answer, then explain.
- Use plain English and short paragraphs.
- Use bullet points for lists of more than three items.

Honesty:
- If you are not sure, say so.
- Do not invent facts, quotes or sources.
- Tell me when a question needs a professional or an official source.

If my request is unclear, ask up to two questions before answering.
```

### Template: study tutor

```
Act as a patient tutor for [subject, level].
Never just give the final answer to practice problems; first give a hint,
then wait for my attempt.
Explain mistakes kindly and show the correct method.
Use simple examples and check my understanding with one question at the end.
```

This kind of setup turns an AI into a practice partner. It supports learning when you want it to, rather than handing you finished work.

### Template: writing editor

```
Act as a careful editor. Preserve my meaning and voice.
Point out unclear sentences, then offer a revised version.
Do not add new claims. List any statement that needs a source.
```

## Writing instructions that actually hold

### Be specific and positive

"Be concise" is soft. "Answer in under 150 words unless I ask for more" is firm. Where possible, say what to do rather than what to avoid.

### Avoid conflicts

If your standing rule says "always give a table" and a later prompt asks for an essay, the AI has to choose. Add a priority line: "Follow my message-level instructions if they conflict with these."

### Keep it short

Long lists dilute the important rules. Start with five to eight lines, test, then refine.

## Testing your instructions

After saving instructions, run three test prompts: a simple question, a task that needs formatting, and an ambiguous request. Check whether the answers reflect your rules. If something is ignored, make that rule shorter and more explicit, or move it earlier in the list.

## Privacy and safety

Do not put passwords, financial details, health records or other sensitive data into standing instructions. Treat saved preferences as visible to the product's provider, and read its privacy information. Review them periodically and remove anything outdated.

## System prompts for people who build things

If you create a chatbot for a club, classroom or small business, the system prompt is where you define scope and boundaries: what topics it covers, how it should respond when it does not know, and when to refer people to a human. Test it with awkward questions and change it based on what you see. Do not rely on a system prompt alone to enforce security or protect private information.

## Examples of standing instructions for different users

A student might write: "I am an undergraduate in biology. Explain at a first-year level, give one real-world example, and finish with a question that tests my understanding. Do not write assignments for me; help me understand and plan."

A job seeker might write: "I am applying for administrative roles. Keep resume and cover letter wording truthful, concise and specific. Never invent achievements. Ask me for missing details instead of guessing."

A small-business owner might write: "I run a two-person bakery. Write in a friendly, local voice. Keep customer messages under 80 words. Mention opening hours only if I provide them."

Each of these is short, specific and mostly positive, which is exactly what makes standing instructions work. They also include a line about honesty and a line about what to do when information is missing, which prevents many invented details.

## Updating instructions as you learn

Treat your instructions as a living document. When you notice that you keep correcting the same thing, such as answers being too long or too formal, add one line to fix it. When a rule no longer helps, remove it. A good rhythm is to review your standing instructions every month or two and ask whether each line still earns its place.

## Common mistakes

- **Writing an essay.** Dense paragraphs of preferences are hard to follow. Use short lines.
- **Mixing temporary and permanent details.** Keep task details in the message.
- **Vague personality instructions.** "Be smart and helpful" adds little.
- **Rules that conflict.** Check for contradictions and set a priority.
- **Forgetting they are on.** Old instructions can shape new answers. Review them.
- **Storing sensitive data.** Keep private information out.

## Next steps

Draft your own standing instructions with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), find persona examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or explore [AI tools](/ai-tools) to see where custom settings are available.

faq.q: What is the difference between a system prompt and a user prompt?
faq.a: A system prompt sets standing rules for the whole conversation, such as role, tone and limits. A user prompt is the individual request you send. System-level guidance shapes every answer, while user prompts describe each specific task.

faq.q: What should I put in custom instructions?
faq.a: Include stable details: your role, preferred reading level, formatting habits, tone, and honesty rules such as saying when unsure. Leave out task-specific details and anything sensitive, like passwords or private records.

faq.q: Why does the AI ignore my custom instructions sometimes?
faq.a: Instructions may be too long, vague or in conflict with your message. Shorten them, make each rule explicit and positive, add a priority line for conflicts, and test with a few sample prompts to see what changes.

faq.q: Are system prompts secure enough to protect secrets?
faq.a: No. A system prompt guides behaviour but should not be treated as a security barrier. Never place confidential data in it, and use proper access controls and privacy settings for anything sensitive.

title: Prompt Templates With Variables: Build Reusable AI Prompts
excerpt: Turn prompts you repeat into reusable templates with fill-in variables. Learn the structure, naming tips and ready-made templates for study, work and writing.
seo_title: Prompt Templates With Variables: Build Reusable AI Prompts
seo_description: Learn how to build prompt templates with variables for reusable AI prompts. Includes bracket syntax, ready-made templates, testing tips and mistakes to avoid.
content:
A prompt template is a saved prompt with blanks, called variables, that you fill in each time. Instead of rewriting a good prompt from scratch, you change only the parts that differ, such as the topic, audience or word limit. This saves time and makes your results more consistent.

If you notice yourself typing nearly the same request every week, you are ready to build a template.

## What a variable is

A variable is a placeholder for information that changes. Most people write them in square brackets, curly braces or capital letters:

- [TOPIC]
- {audience}
- <<word_limit>>

The symbols do not matter to the AI. What matters is that you know which blanks to replace and that no placeholder is left in the final prompt by accident.

## Anatomy of a good template

A reliable template has three layers:

1. **Fixed instructions.** The parts that never change: role, method, rules.
2. **Variables.** The few details that change each time.
3. **Output format.** A stable structure so results are easy to compare and reuse.

### Example: explainer template

```
You are a clear, patient teacher.

Explain [TOPIC] to [AUDIENCE] in about [WORD_COUNT] words.

Structure:
1. One-sentence definition.
2. A simple analogy from everyday life.
3. A short example.
4. Two common misunderstandings.

Use plain English and define any technical term.
```

Filled in: TOPIC = "inflation", AUDIENCE = "teenagers saving their first pay", WORD_COUNT = "200." You now have a precise prompt in under a minute.

## Choosing good variables

### Keep the number small

Three to six variables is usually plenty. More than that and filling the template becomes a chore, which defeats the purpose.

### Make names descriptive

[AUDIENCE] is better than [X]. When you return to a template months later, clear names tell you exactly what to enter.

### Offer defaults

Add a default in parentheses so you can skip blanks you rarely change:

```
Tone: [TONE, default: friendly and clear]
Length: [LENGTH, default: 150 words]
```

### Separate required from optional

Mark optional fields so you know what you can leave out. Delete unused lines before sending so the AI does not see stray placeholders.

## Templates for common tasks

### Study summary

```
Summarise the notes below for revision.

Subject: [SUBJECT]
Level: [LEVEL, e.g. first-year university]
Output: [NUMBER] key points, then [NUMBER] practice questions without answers.
Use only the notes. Flag anything unclear.

"""
[NOTES]
"""
```

### Professional email

```
Write an email.
From: [YOUR ROLE]
To: [RECIPIENT AND RELATIONSHIP]
Goal: [WHAT YOU WANT THEM TO DO]
Key facts: [DATES, NAMES, NUMBERS]
Tone: [TONE]
Length: under [WORD_COUNT] words. Include a clear subject line.
```

### Resume bullet improver

```
Improve this resume bullet for a [JOB TITLE] application.
Keep it truthful: do not add achievements or numbers I did not give.
Start with a strong action verb, show the result if one is given, and keep
it under 25 words.
Original: [BULLET]
Give three versions.
```

### Lesson idea generator

```
Suggest [NUMBER] activities for teaching [SKILL] to [GRADE/AGE GROUP].
Each activity: name, 10-minute outline, materials, and one way to check
understanding. Limit to resources found in a typical classroom.
```

## Organising your templates

Keep them somewhere you can find them in seconds: a notes app, a document with headings or a spreadsheet with one row per template. Useful columns are name, purpose, the template text, and notes on what worked. Group them by task type rather than by tool, so they stay useful if you switch AI products.

## Testing a template

Before you rely on a template, test it with two or three different inputs:

1. Fill it with an easy case. Does the output match the format?
2. Fill it with an awkward case, such as a very short or very long input. Does it break?
3. Read the output for stray placeholders or rules that were ignored.

Revise and add a version note, such as "v2: added word limit." Over time your best templates become small, dependable tools.

## Templates and good judgment

A template makes the AI more predictable, not more correct. You still need to check facts, adapt the output to your situation and use it in line with your school or workplace rules. Avoid templates that encourage handing off thinking you are supposed to do yourself, such as generating a whole graded essay to submit as your own.

## Building your first template in five minutes

Pick a prompt you have used at least twice. Paste your best version into a note and then highlight every detail that changed between uses. Replace each highlighted detail with a bracketed name. Add a short format section if there was not one. That is your first template.

For example, a student who regularly asks for a revision schedule might notice that the subject, exam date and weekly hours always change. Their template becomes: "Create a revision schedule for [SUBJECT] with the exam on [EXAM_DATE]. I can study [HOURS] hours per week. Use a weekly table with topic, task and a short review slot." The same structure serves every course.

## Variables for audience and tone

Two of the most valuable variables are [AUDIENCE] and [TONE]. They are easy to forget and they change results more than almost anything else. Placing them near the top of the template makes you fill them in every time. If you find that you always use the same tone, turn it into fixed text and remove the variable to keep the template lean.

## Sharing templates with others

Templates are easy to share with classmates, colleagues or a team, which helps everyone get similar quality. When you share one, include a short note on what each variable expects, with an example value. A line such as "[LEVEL]: e.g., Year 9, first-year university, beginner" prevents misuse. Ask others to report which variable they found confusing, then improve the wording.

## Handling optional blocks

Some details only apply sometimes, such as an example, a word limit or a list of banned phrases. Write these as clearly marked optional lines, for instance "(Optional) Avoid these phrases: [LIST]". Before sending, either fill them in or delete the whole line. This habit keeps one template flexible enough to cover quick requests and detailed ones, so you do not need to maintain two near-identical versions of the same prompt.

## Common mistakes

- **Too many variables.** Filling the template takes longer than writing a prompt.
- **Unclear names.** Future you will not remember what [INPUT2] means.
- **Leaving placeholders in.** Always scan before sending.
- **Never updating.** Improve the template when you find a better wording.
- **One template for everything.** Create separate templates for separate tasks.
- **No format section.** Without it, outputs vary and are harder to reuse.

## Next steps

Create and refine your own versions with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), see ready-made examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or save time on applications with the [resume builder](/resume-builder).

faq.q: What is a prompt template?
faq.a: A prompt template is a saved prompt with placeholders, called variables, for the details that change, such as topic, audience and length. You fill in the blanks each time, which keeps results consistent and saves rewriting.

faq.q: How many variables should a template have?
faq.a: Usually three to six. Too few and the template is rigid; too many and filling it in becomes a chore. Use descriptive names and defaults for details you rarely change.

faq.q: Where should I store my prompt templates?
faq.a: Use any place you can search quickly: a notes app, a document with headings or a spreadsheet. Group by task type, note what worked, and keep version labels so you can improve them over time.

faq.q: Do templates make AI answers more accurate?
faq.a: Templates make format and approach more consistent, but not automatically more correct. You still need to provide accurate inputs, check the facts in the output, and adapt the result to your own situation and purpose.

title: 10 Common Prompt Engineering Mistakes Beginners Make
excerpt: Weak AI answers usually trace back to a handful of prompt mistakes. Learn the ten most common ones, why they hurt results, and how to fix each with examples.
seo_title: 10 Common Prompt Engineering Mistakes Beginners Make
seo_description: Avoid the 10 most common prompt engineering mistakes beginners make, from vague requests to missing context, with before-and-after fixes and a quick checklist.
content:
The most common prompt engineering mistakes are being vague, leaving out context, asking for too much at once, skipping the format, and accepting the first answer without checking it. Each one is easy to fix once you can recognise it, and fixing them usually improves results more than any clever trick.

Here are ten mistakes in rough order of how often they cause trouble, with a before-and-after for each.

## 1. Being too vague

**Before:** "Tell me about marketing."

**After:** "Explain three low-cost marketing methods for a new local bakery, with one example action for each."

Vague prompts get broad, generic answers because the AI has to guess your purpose. Name the subject, audience and goal.

## 2. Leaving out context

The AI cannot see your situation. If you are a beginner, say so. If you have a deadline, a budget or a draft, include it.

**Before:** "How should I prepare for the interview?"

**After:** "I have a 30-minute interview for an entry-level data analyst role next Tuesday. I know basic spreadsheets but not SQL. Suggest a three-day preparation plan."

## 3. Asking for several things at once

"Summarise this article, critique it, write a rebuttal, and make a quiz" asks for four jobs. Quality drops when tasks compete. Split them into steps, or number them clearly and review each result.

## 4. Not specifying the format

If you do not say how the answer should look, you get whatever the model prefers, often long paragraphs. Ask for what you need: a table, a checklist, five bullets, an email with a subject line.

## 5. Ignoring the audience

An explanation for a ten-year-old differs from one for a specialist. Add "for [audience]" to almost every request. It is one of the quickest ways to adjust vocabulary, depth and examples.

## 6. Giving conflicting instructions

"Be extremely detailed, but keep it under 40 words" cannot be satisfied. Re-read your prompt for contradictions. If both goals matter, ask for two outputs: a short version and a detailed version.

## 7. Accepting the first answer

The first reply is a draft. Ask for changes: "Make the second point more specific," "Shorten to 100 words," "Add a counter-example." Iteration is part of the method, not an extra step.

## 8. Trusting every fact

AI can produce confident statements that are wrong, outdated or invented, including names, dates, quotes and references. Treat factual claims as leads to verify. Ask it to flag uncertain claims, and check important details against official or reliable sources.

## 9. Overloading with background

The opposite of leaving out context is dumping a huge amount of loosely relevant text. This can bury the key instruction. Include what matters, remove what does not, and place your main request clearly, ideally near the start and repeated briefly at the end.

## 10. Never saving what works

Many beginners solve the same problem again and again. When a prompt works, save it with a note about when to use it. Turn recurring prompts into templates with blanks for the details that change.

## A before-and-after in full

**Weak prompt:**

> Write an essay about social media.

**Improved prompt:**

```
I am a college student writing a 500-word discussion post for an
introductory sociology class. The question is: "How has social media changed
the way young people form friendships?"

Help me plan, not write the final text:
1. Suggest a thesis statement in two versions (one balanced, one critical).
2. Give an outline with three main points and the kind of evidence I should look for.
3. List two counter-arguments I should address.

Do not invent statistics or sources; I will find my own.
```

The improved version defines the task, level and word count, asks for planning help rather than finished text and keeps the thinking and writing in the student's hands. It also blocks invented evidence.

## A ten-second pre-send checklist

Before you press send, scan these questions:

- Is my goal stated in one clear sentence?
- Did I say who the answer is for?
- Did I give the background the AI cannot know?
- Did I choose a format and a length?
- Are there any contradictions?
- Is there only one main task?

If all six are yes, your prompt is in good shape.

## Why these mistakes are so common

Most of them come from the same root: we write prompts the way we think, in shorthand. Inside our own heads, "make it better" has a clear meaning. On the screen, it has none. The skill of prompt engineering is partly the habit of translating private shorthand into explicit language. That habit also improves your emails, briefs and instructions to people, which is a nice side benefit.

Another reason is the expectation that AI should "just know." Tools are impressive, so it feels unfair to explain things at length. But a short extra sentence costs you seconds and often saves minutes of rework.

## Mistakes with responsibility

Some errors are not about quality but about how you use the tool:

- **Submitting AI output as your own graded work** when rules forbid it. Check your school's or employer's policy and use AI to learn, plan and review.
- **Pasting private or confidential information** such as personal data of other people, passwords or sensitive documents.
- **Using output without review** in situations where mistakes matter, such as health, legal or financial decisions. Consult qualified professionals for those.

## How to practise fixing mistakes

Take three of your old prompts that gave poor results. Mark which of the ten mistakes each contained. Rewrite them, run them again and compare. This simple exercise teaches faster than reading advice, because you see the effect on your own tasks.

## Common mistakes in the middle of a conversation

Some errors appear only after the first message. One is changing direction without saying so: you ask about a cover letter, then suddenly request a recipe, and the AI blends the two contexts. Announce topic changes clearly or open a new chat. Another is correcting the AI with emotion instead of information. "That is wrong" gives no direction, while "The second paragraph claims the deadline is May; it is June" gives the model something to fix.

A third is forgetting that the AI does not remember your earlier chats unless a tool specifically provides that feature. If it matters, restate the key facts. Check the official help pages of your tool to see what it retains.

## Turning mistakes into habits

The goal is not perfection but a better default. After a few weeks of deliberate practice, you will find yourself adding audience, format and limits without thinking. Keep a short note of your personal top three mistakes, such as "forgot format" or "no audience," and glance at it before important prompts. Personal reminders work better than a long list of rules you try to memorise.

## Next steps

Build clearer requests with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), study well-formed examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or check out [student prompts](/prompts/category/students) that avoid these pitfalls.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake beginners make with AI prompts?
faq.a: Being vague. Short requests like 'tell me about marketing' leave audience, purpose, length and format open, so the AI returns something generic. Adding context, a clear task and a format fixes most weak answers.

faq.q: Why does the AI give me generic answers?
faq.a: Generic answers usually mean the prompt lacked specifics. Add who the answer is for, your situation, a clear task, a format and a limit. Then follow up with targeted changes rather than starting from scratch.

faq.q: Should I fact-check AI answers?
faq.a: Yes. AI can state wrong or invented details with confidence. Verify names, dates, statistics, quotes and references using reliable sources, especially for school, work or any decision where a mistake could matter.

faq.q: How can I avoid asking for too much in one prompt?
faq.a: Write one main task per message. If you need several outputs, number the steps and review each in turn, or run them as separate prompts. This keeps answers focused and easier to correct.

title: How to Write Clear AI Prompts: A 7-Point Checklist
excerpt: A clear AI prompt names the goal, audience, context, format, length, tone and limits. Use this seven-point checklist, with examples, to improve any prompt fast.
seo_title: How to Write Clear AI Prompts: A 7-Point Checklist
seo_description: Use this 7-point checklist to write clear AI prompts: goal, audience, context, format, length, tone and limits, with before-and-after examples and a template.
content:
A clear AI prompt states seven things: the goal, the audience, the context, the format, the length, the tone and any limits. You do not need all seven every time, but running through them takes under a minute and catches the gaps that cause weak answers.

This checklist works for any task, from drafting an email to planning a study week. Each point is explained below with a small example, followed by a template you can copy.

## 1. Goal: what do you want at the end?

Describe the result, not just the topic. "Photosynthesis" is a topic. "A one-page explanation of photosynthesis I can use to revise for tomorrow's quiz" is a goal. The goal tells the AI what success looks like.

A useful trick: finish the sentence "When this is done, I will use it to..." and put the answer in your prompt.

## 2. Audience: who is it for?

Audience controls vocabulary, depth and examples. Specify age, experience level or role: "for a complete beginner," "for my manager, who is busy," "for Year 7 students." If the audience is you, say what you already know.

## 3. Context: what does the AI not know?

Context includes your situation, constraints and source material. Ask yourself what a helpful stranger would need to ask before they could start. Include:

- the situation or background
- anything you have already tried
- relevant text or notes you paste in
- deadlines or practical limits

## 4. Format: what shape should the answer take?

Choose a structure you can use immediately: numbered steps, a table, a checklist, a short email, headings with paragraphs. If you will copy it into a document or spreadsheet, say so.

## 5. Length: how much?

Use numbers: "under 150 words," "five bullet points," "two paragraphs." Numbers are testable, and they stop answers from running on. If you need depth, say how much: "about 600 words with three sections."

## 6. Tone: how should it sound?

Pick two or three qualities, such as "friendly and direct" or "formal and precise." Tone matters most for messages that go to real people. For study notes, "simple and neutral" may be enough.

## 7. Limits: what should be avoided or restricted?

Limits can concern scope ("only cover the causes"), sources ("use only the text below") and style ("no jargon"). They also protect accuracy: "Do not invent quotes or statistics; say if you do not know."

## The seven points in one template

```
Goal: [What I want to end up with and how I will use it]
Audience: [Who will read/use it and what they already know]
Context: [Background, my situation, pasted material]
Format: [Table / steps / email / bullets / headings]
Length: [Number of words, items or paragraphs]
Tone: [Two or three qualities]
Limits: [What to include, exclude or avoid]
```

You can paste this into any chat and fill in the lines that matter.

## Example: from vague to clear

**Vague:**

> Help me write an email to my teacher.

**Clear:**

```
Goal: Ask my teacher for a three-day extension on my history essay.
Audience: Mr Ahmed, a teacher who values honesty and early notice.
Context: The essay is due Friday. I was ill on Monday and Tuesday and have
a doctor's note. I have completed the research and outline.
Format: A short email with a subject line.
Length: Under 120 words.
Tone: Polite, honest, not overly apologetic.
Limits: Do not make excuses I did not mention; do not promise anything
beyond the new deadline.
```

Notice the "limits" line. It keeps the AI from adding invented reasons, which protects your honesty.

## Quick tests for clarity

After you write a prompt, try these checks:

1. **The stranger test.** Would a capable person who knows nothing about your situation understand what to do?
2. **The finish-line test.** Could you recognise when the answer is done and good?
3. **The one-task test.** Can you describe the request in a single sentence?
4. **The contradiction test.** Do any two lines pull in opposite directions?

If a check fails, edit the prompt rather than hoping the AI will work it out.

## Using the checklist for different goals

### Learning

Add your current level and ask for explanations plus practice: "Explain, then give me three questions to test myself without answers."

### Writing

Add the purpose and reader, and ask for outline first, draft second. That keeps you in control of the ideas.

### Decisions

List your criteria and constraints, ask for pros and cons for each option and request that assumptions be stated.

### Job applications

Provide the real job description and your true experience, and require that the AI not invent achievements. Review everything for accuracy before sending.

## When shorter is fine

A clear prompt is not always long. "Give me five synonyms for 'important' suitable for a formal report" is complete. The checklist is a tool to find what is missing, not a form you must always fill out. If the task is simple, a single line may satisfy all seven points implicitly.

## A worked example for learning

Suppose you are studying economics and type: "Explain supply and demand." Run the checklist. Goal: understand it well enough to answer exam questions. Audience: you, a first-year student who has seen the graph but not the reasoning. Context: the exam includes short-answer questions on price changes. Format: a short explanation, one worked example and three practice questions. Length: about 300 words plus questions. Tone: simple and encouraging. Limits: no advanced mathematics, and no answers to the practice questions until you attempt them.

Put together, that becomes a prompt of five or six lines that produces a study resource instead of a textbook paragraph. The extra effort was about sixty seconds.

## Building the habit

Practice the checklist on three everyday prompts this week. Write the short version first, then the checklist version, and compare the answers. You will probably find that two or three of the seven points do most of the work for your type of task. Keep those as your personal short list. For many people it is audience, format and limits.

## Common mistakes

- **Describing the topic but not the goal.** Say what you will do with the output.
- **Using relative words like "short" and "simple."** Use numbers and examples.
- **Forgetting the audience.** It is the cheapest improvement available.
- **Letting limits stay unspoken.** If you do not want jargon or invented facts, say so.
- **Writing one giant paragraph.** Use labelled lines so you can scan and edit.
- **Skipping the review.** Read the answer for accuracy and fit before using it.

## Next steps

Fill in a structured request with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), explore finished examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or save time on study planning with [productivity prompts](/prompts/category/productivity).

faq.q: What makes an AI prompt clear?
faq.a: A clear prompt names the goal, audience and context, states the format and length, and sets any limits on tone, scope or sources. A capable stranger should understand what to do from the prompt alone.

faq.q: Do I need all seven checklist points in every prompt?
faq.a: No. Simple tasks may need only a goal and a format. Use the checklist as a quick scan to find gaps when answers feel generic, off-tone, too long or poorly organised for what you intended.

faq.q: How long should a good prompt be?
faq.a: As long as needed to cover the essentials, and no longer. Many strong prompts are three to eight lines. Focus on relevant detail and clear structure rather than counting words or padding the request.

faq.q: Can I turn this checklist into a reusable template?
faq.a: Yes. Save the seven labelled lines in a notes app and fill in what applies each time. Remove unused lines before sending so the AI does not see empty placeholders or conflicting leftovers.

title: How Much Context to Give AI: What to Include and Skip
excerpt: Too little context gives generic answers; too much buries the point. Learn what background to include in an AI prompt, what to skip, and how to structure it.
seo_title: How Much Context to Give AI: What to Include and Skip
seo_description: Learn how much context to give AI in a prompt. See what background to include, what to skip, how to paste source text, and use a simple context template.
content:
Give the AI the background it cannot guess and that changes the answer: your goal, your audience, key facts, source material and limits. Leave out unrelated history, repeated details and anything that would not change what a good answer looks like.

Context is the single biggest quality lever in prompting, yet most people either give none or paste far too much. This guide shows you how to find the right amount.

## What counts as context

Context is every piece of information that helps the AI understand your situation. It falls into five groups:

1. **Purpose:** why you need the answer and what you will do with it.
2. **Audience:** who will read or use it.
3. **Situation:** relevant facts about you, the project or the setting.
4. **Material:** text, notes, data or examples you provide.
5. **Constraints:** deadlines, resources, length limits, rules.

If you can answer these five points in a few lines, you have enough context for most tasks.

## The "helpful stranger" test

Imagine sending your prompt to a friendly expert who has never met you. What would they ask before starting? Those questions point to missing context. For example, for the request "plan my week," a stranger would ask: What are your commitments? What are your goals? When do you have energy? Add those answers up front and you skip the back-and-forth.

## What to include

### Facts that change the advice

If you are a beginner, say it. If you have two hours a day, say it. If you are working in a country with different rules or a specific curriculum, name it. These details change the recommendation.

### Examples of what you like

A short sample of the style, structure or quality you want gives more guidance than a paragraph of adjectives.

### Previous attempts

"I tried reading the textbook twice and it did not stick" helps the AI suggest a different approach rather than repeating your failed one.

### Definitions of your own terms

If you use a nickname for a project or a course code, define it. The AI cannot know what "Plan B" means.

## What to skip

- **Unrelated backstory.** Your life story rarely helps a request for a recipe substitution.
- **Duplicate information.** Saying the same thing three ways adds length, not clarity.
- **Sensitive data.** Avoid names, addresses, ID numbers, passwords and confidential business details. Replace them with generic placeholders like "Client A."
- **Unneeded documents.** Paste the relevant section, not the whole file.

## How to structure context

A clear structure helps both you and the AI. Put context first, task second, format third, and label each part:

```
CONTEXT
- I am a second-year nursing student.
- I have an exam in 10 days on pharmacology basics.
- I learn best from examples and short quizzes.

TASK
Create a 10-day revision plan focusing on drug classes and common
side effects.

FORMAT
A table with day, topic, 30-minute activity and a 5-question self-quiz.
Note: this is a study aid; I will confirm clinical details in my textbook.
```

Labels make the prompt easy to scan and easy to modify later.

## Pasting source text

When you want the AI to work with a document, paste it with clear boundaries and an instruction about how to use it:

```
Use only the text between the triple quotes to answer.
If the answer is not in the text, say "Not in the text."

"""
[paste excerpt]
"""

Question: What are the three main causes of the decline described?
```

For long materials, break them into sections and work through them one at a time, or ask for a section-by-section summary first and then ask follow-up questions. Models can lose track of details in very long inputs, so verify key points against the original.

## Context across a long conversation

In a long chat, early information can fade or get contradicted. Help by:

- restating key facts when you change direction
- summarising progress: "So far we agreed on A and B. Now help me with C."
- starting a new chat for a new topic and pasting a short summary

A tidy, short summary is often more effective than scrolling back through pages of history.

## Balancing detail and focus

A good test is relevance. Ask of each sentence, "Would the answer change if I removed this?" If no, cut it. If yes, keep it. Some tasks genuinely need long context, such as analysing a case study, and that is fine as long as it is organised and relevant.

## Context and privacy

Because you often share context in a prompt, think about what you are comfortable sharing. Anonymise people and organisations, remove identifying numbers and read the privacy settings of the tool you use. If a document is confidential at work or school, check policy before pasting it.

## Examples of too little, too much and just right

**Too little:** "Write a speech."

**Too much:** three paragraphs about your school's history, your family, last year's event and your feelings, followed by "write a speech."

**Just right:** "Write a two-minute speech for the school awards evening, thanking volunteers. Audience: parents and teachers. Include one light joke and mention the new library project. Warm, sincere tone."

The third version holds only what shapes the speech: length, occasion, audience, content points and tone.

## Asking the AI what it needs

If you are unsure what context to provide, ask. A simple prompt works: "I want help planning a presentation on renewable energy. What information do you need from me to do this well?" The AI will list questions about audience, time, level and goals. Answer them in a single reply and then ask for the plan. This is a good way to learn which context matters for your type of task, and over time you will start including those items automatically.

## Updating context as you go

Context is not fixed. If the audience changes or you discover a new constraint, say so: "Update: the presentation is now 5 minutes, not 10." A short, explicit update is better than hoping the AI infers the change from the conversation.

## Common mistakes

- **Assuming the AI knows your situation.** It does not, beyond what is in the chat.
- **Pasting everything.** Irrelevant text hides the key request.
- **Burying the task.** State the main request clearly, not in the middle of a long paragraph.
- **Giving outdated context.** If facts change mid-chat, say so.
- **Sharing sensitive information.** Replace private details with placeholders.
- **Not labelling parts.** Unlabelled blocks of text blur instructions and material.

## Next steps

Structure your background with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), find context-rich examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or plan study sessions around your own schedule with the [Study Planner](/study-planner).

faq.q: How much context should I give an AI?
faq.a: Give enough to answer the helpful-stranger test: purpose, audience, key facts, source material and limits. Skip unrelated backstory and repeated details. A few focused lines usually beat pages of loosely relevant text.

faq.q: Can I paste a whole document into an AI chat?
faq.a: Often you can, but results improve when you paste only the relevant sections with clear boundaries and instructions. Check privacy rules first and verify key details against the original document.

faq.q: Why does the AI forget earlier details in a long chat?
faq.a: Long conversations can dilute or contradict earlier information. Restate important facts, summarise progress before changing direction, or start a new chat with a short summary of the details that matter.

faq.q: Should I include personal information as context?
faq.a: Include only what the task needs and avoid sensitive data such as passwords, ID numbers or confidential details. Use placeholders like 'Client A' and read the tool's privacy information before sharing.

title: Output Format Prompts: Get Tables, Lists, Steps and JSON
excerpt: Tell AI how to format answers so you can use them at once. Learn prompts for tables, bullet lists, step-by-step guides, emails and simple JSON, with examples.
seo_title: Output Format Prompts: Get Tables, Lists, Steps and JSON
seo_description: Learn how to write output format prompts for tables, bullet lists, numbered steps, email drafts and simple JSON, with copy-ready examples and mistakes to avoid.
content:
To get an AI answer in the shape you need, name the format explicitly and describe its parts: for a table, list the column names; for steps, say how many and how detailed; for data, show an example of the structure. Format instructions turn a block of text into something you can paste straight into a document, spreadsheet or app.

Format is the easiest prompt improvement to apply, because you decide what the finished product looks like before the AI starts.

## Why format deserves its own line

When you do not specify a format, the AI picks its own, usually flowing paragraphs. That is fine for explanation but awkward for comparison, planning or data. Asking for a format also forces the answer to be organised, which often improves quality as well as readability.

## Bullet lists

Use bullet lists for ideas, features or summaries.

```
List the main benefits of spaced repetition for a student.
Format: 5 bullet points, each starting with a bold keyword and followed by
one sentence of no more than 20 words.
```

Specify the count and length of each bullet, or you may get twelve rambling items.

## Numbered steps

Use numbered steps for procedures.

```
Explain how to set up a weekly study routine.
Format: 6 numbered steps. Each step has a short title and one sentence
describing what to do. Finish with a "Common problem and fix" line.
```

For tasks where the order matters, such as a recipe or a setup guide, ask for steps rather than prose.

## Tables

Tables are ideal for comparisons. Name the columns, the rows and any cell rules.

```
Compare three note-taking methods: Cornell, mind map and outline.
Format: a table with columns Method, Best for, Main strength, Main
weakness. Keep each cell under 12 words.
```

If you plan to paste the table into a spreadsheet, you can ask for "a Markdown table" or "values separated by commas." Check the result for alignment and accuracy before relying on it.

## Headings and sections

For longer pieces, specify the headings so the structure matches your needs:

```
Write a one-page briefing on remote work for a small team.
Use these headings in order: Summary, Benefits, Risks, Recommendations.
Under each heading, write no more than three sentences.
```

## Email and message formats

Describe the parts of the message:

```
Draft an email to a customer who received a late delivery.
Format: subject line; greeting; two short paragraphs (apology and fix);
one-sentence closing with a clear next step. Under 110 words.
```

## Simple JSON or structured data

If you are working with data, a spreadsheet or a small app, you can request a structured output. Show the structure you want:

```
Extract the details from the text below and return them as JSON with these
keys: "name", "date", "location", "action_needed".
If a detail is missing, use null. Return only the JSON, with no explanation.

Text: """[paste text]"""
```

Always validate the output. Models sometimes add extra text or small syntax mistakes, and a missing comma can break a program. If you build something important, use a JSON validator and consult the official documentation of the tool you use for features that enforce structure.

## Combining formats

You can mix formats in one answer: a two-sentence summary, a table of options and a three-step plan. Label the sections so the response stays predictable:

```
Section 1: Summary (2 sentences)
Section 2: Options table (columns: Option, Cost, Effort, Risk)
Section 3: Recommendation (3 bullets)
```

## Adding an example of the format

When structure is complicated, show a tiny example row or layout:

```
Return each flashcard in this format:
Q: [question]
A: [answer under 20 words]
Hint: [one clue]
```

The AI will usually follow your pattern closely. This is a light version of few-shot prompting.

## Controlling extras

Models often add introductions such as "Sure, here is your table." If that gets in the way, add "Return only the table, with no introduction or closing remarks." For answers you will paste elsewhere, this saves cleanup time.

## Format for accessibility and readability

Short paragraphs, clear headings and descriptive labels help every reader. If your audience includes people who use screen readers or read on small screens, avoid complex nested tables and ask for simple lists instead.

## Choosing the right format for the job

Match the format to what you intend to do with the answer:

- **To compare options:** table.
- **To follow a process:** numbered steps.
- **To remember ideas:** bullets or flashcards.
- **To send to someone:** email or message with subject line.
- **To process in a spreadsheet or program:** comma-separated values or simple JSON.
- **To read and think:** short paragraphs with headings.

If you are unsure, ask for two formats and see which is more useful. Over time you will develop preferences, and you can add them to your standing instructions so you do not repeat them.

## Fixing a format that went wrong

If the AI ignores your format, avoid starting over. Reply with a direct correction: "Reformat the above as a table with columns A, B and C. Do not change the content." Asking for a pure reformat keeps the content stable and changes only the shape. If the format keeps failing, simplify it. Complex nested structures are harder to follow than a flat list, and a simpler layout is often more readable anyway.

## Format prompts for students and teachers

Students can ask for revision material in structures that support recall: a two-column table of term and definition, a timeline in numbered steps, or a list of questions with a space for their own answers. Teachers can request a lesson outline with fixed headings (objective, activity, materials, check for understanding) so that every plan they generate has the same layout. In both cases, a fixed structure makes the output easier to compare, store and improve, and it keeps your attention on the content rather than on formatting.

## Common mistakes

- **Not naming columns or fields.** The AI invents them, and they may not match your needs.
- **Asking for a table with too many columns.** Four or five is usually readable.
- **Forgetting length limits per cell or bullet.** Cells fill up with long sentences.
- **Trusting structured data blindly.** Check values and syntax.
- **Requesting a format that does not suit the content.** A story does not need a table.
- **Leaving in the chatty intro.** Ask for only the formatted output if you will paste it.

## Next steps

Specify your preferred layout using the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), browse format-ready examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or turn lists into schedules with the [Study Planner](/study-planner).

faq.a: Ask for a table and name the columns, such as Method, Best for, Strength and Weakness. Add limits like 'keep each cell under 12 words' and check the result for accuracy before you use it.

faq.q: Can AI return data as JSON?
faq.a: Yes, if you show the keys you want and say 'return only the JSON'. Always validate the output, since small syntax errors or extra text can occur, especially if you plan to feed it into a program.

faq.q: How do I stop the AI adding an introduction?
faq.a: Add an instruction such as 'Return only the table, with no introduction or closing remarks.' This is useful when you will copy the answer directly into a document or spreadsheet.

faq.q: What is the best format for study notes?
faq.a: It depends on your goal. Bullet lists suit summaries, tables suit comparisons, and question-and-answer pairs suit flashcards. Specify the structure and length so notes stay scannable and easy to review.

title: How to Fix Vague, Generic AI Answers: 8 Prompt Fixes
excerpt: Getting bland, generic answers from AI? Use these eight prompt fixes, from adding audience and examples to demanding specifics, with before-and-after examples.
seo_title: How to Fix Vague, Generic AI Answers: 8 Prompt Fixes
seo_description: Fix vague, generic AI answers with eight prompt changes: add audience, context, constraints, examples and critique steps, with before-and-after prompts.
content:
Vague, generic AI answers almost always come from vague prompts. To fix them, add a specific audience, concrete context, a clear format, limits, an example of what you want and a request for specifics, then refine with targeted follow-ups. The eight fixes below work on almost any task.

Generic output has a cause: when the prompt leaves many choices open, the model picks the most common, safest option. Your job is to close those choices on purpose.

## Fix 1: Name the audience

Audience is the fastest correction. Compare:

- "Explain budgeting."
- "Explain budgeting to a first-year university student with a part-time job and irregular income."

The second prompt immediately suggests examples, tone and level. Whenever you read an answer and think "this is not for me," add the real audience.

## Fix 2: Add your real situation

Generic advice comes from generic inputs. Include facts such as your level, resources, time and constraints.

**Before:** "How can I learn Spanish?"

**After:** "I have 20 minutes a day, a commute of 30 minutes on public transport, and I want to hold basic conversations in six months. Suggest a weekly routine."

## Fix 3: Ask for specifics, not general advice

Phrases such as "give concrete examples," "name the exact steps" and "avoid general advice" push the model away from platitudes.

```
Give me five specific actions I can take this week to improve my
presentation skills. Each action must be something I can finish in
under 30 minutes and must include an example.
```

## Fix 4: Show an example of what you want

If you have a sample of the style or depth you like, include it. You can also describe the opposite: "Avoid the style of this example: [generic sentence]." Examples give the AI something firm to aim at, which generic instructions cannot.

## Fix 5: Set constraints that force choices

Tight limits remove padding. "Maximum 100 words" forces prioritisation. "Choose only the top three" forces a ranking. "Do not include introductory or summarising sentences" removes filler.

## Fix 6: Ask for trade-offs and reasons

Bland answers often list options with no judgment. Ask the AI to compare, rank and justify:

```
Recommend one of these three study methods for me and explain why.
Then explain what would make you recommend a different one.
Use my situation: [details].
```

Being asked to justify a choice pushes the response toward reasoning rather than listing.

## Fix 7: Request a critique, then a rewrite

Use the AI as its own editor. After the first answer, say:

```
Critique your answer: where is it generic, vague or missing detail?
List three weaknesses, then rewrite it to fix them.
```

This two-step approach often surfaces improvements you would not have specified yourself.

## Fix 8: Provide the missing facts and let the AI ask

Sometimes the AI is vague because it has too little information. Invite questions:

```
Before you answer, ask me up to five questions that would help you give
a more specific, useful response. Wait for my replies.
```

This turns a one-way request into a short interview and often produces much better output.

## A complete before-and-after

**Before:**

> Give me tips for writing a good resume.

The result is a familiar list of general tips.

**After:**

```
I am a recent graduate in environmental science applying for entry-level
roles at conservation charities. I have one internship (3 months), a final
year project on river water quality, and volunteer work with a local
clean-up group.

Give me five specific changes I can make to my resume to suit these roles.
For each, show a short before-and-after example using my experience. Do not
invent achievements or numbers; use placeholders like [number] where I need
to add real data.
```

Now the answer can be about the person, and the instruction against invented details protects honesty.

## Diagnosing the type of vagueness

Not all vagueness is the same. Quick diagnosis helps you choose a fix:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feels like a textbook intro | No audience or situation | Fixes 1, 2 |
| Long list of obvious tips | No constraints | Fixes 3, 5 |
| Wrong tone or style | No example | Fix 4 |
| No clear recommendation | No request to choose | Fix 6 |
| Plausible but shallow | No critique step | Fixes 7, 8 |

## Verify before you rely

A more specific answer is not necessarily a more accurate one. When the AI gives names, numbers or claims, check them against reliable sources, especially if you will cite or act on them. Ask it to mark claims that need verification.

## Fixing generic answers in specific subjects

Different tasks tend to produce different kinds of blandness. In writing, the AI often defaults to cliches and neutral phrasing, so ask for concrete details from your own experience and ban stock phrases. In study help, it often gives textbook-style definitions, so ask for analogies, worked examples and practice questions at your level. In career help, it gives widely repeated advice, so supply the job description, your real experience and the specific role you want.

In each case the principle is the same: replace the average with the particular. The more particular facts you provide, the less the model has to fill in with filler.

## Knowing when to stop adjusting the prompt

If you have added audience, context and constraints and the answer is still weak, the topic may need information the AI does not have, such as local rules, recent events or details of your private situation. In that case, supply the source material yourself or consult an authoritative source directly. A prompt cannot create knowledge that is not available, and good judgment includes recognising that limit.

## A quick routine to apply today

When an answer disappoints you, do not delete the chat. Reply with a three-part message: say what is wrong in one sentence, add the missing fact or constraint, and state the change you want. For example: "This is too general. I am a beginner with ten hours a week. Give me three specific steps for the first month, each under 25 words." That single follow-up usually does more than rewriting the whole prompt from the beginning.

## Common mistakes

- **Rewriting the whole prompt each time.** Add one fix at a time and see its effect.
- **Blaming the tool first.** Check whether the prompt left decisions open.
- **Adding adjectives instead of facts.** "Detailed" and "specific" help less than real details.
- **Skipping the follow-up.** Many generic answers become useful after one critique round.
- **Giving no real data.** If you have no facts to supply, ask the AI to ask you.
- **Treating specifics as proof.** Detail can sound confident and still be wrong.

## Next steps

Sharpen your wording with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), explore detailed examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or apply specificity to applications with [career prompts](/prompts/category/careers).

faq.q: Why are AI answers so generic?
faq.a: When a prompt leaves audience, situation, format and limits open, the model defaults to common, safe content. Adding specific context, constraints and examples closes those choices and produces more tailored answers.

faq.q: What is the quickest way to get more specific AI answers?
faq.a: Name the audience and your real situation, then ask for concrete examples and set limits such as a word count or top-three ranking. A follow-up asking the AI to critique and rewrite also helps.

faq.q: Can I ask the AI to ask me questions first?
faq.a: Yes. Add 'Before answering, ask me up to five questions that would help you be more specific.' This fills information gaps and usually leads to a more useful, personalised response.

faq.q: Does a more specific answer mean it is accurate?
faq.a: No. Specific details can still be wrong or invented. Verify names, numbers and claims with reliable sources, and ask the AI to flag statements that need checking before you rely on them.

title: Positive vs Negative Prompts: What to Tell AI to Do
excerpt: Telling AI what to avoid often backfires. Learn when negative instructions work and how to rephrase them as positive ones, with before-and-after examples.
seo_title: Positive vs Negative Prompts: What to Tell AI to Do
seo_description: Learn why 'do not' instructions often fail in AI prompts, when negatives still help, and how to rewrite them as positive instructions with examples.
content:
It is usually more effective to tell an AI what to do than what not to do. Positive instructions such as "use plain words and short sentences" give the model a clear target, while bare prohibitions such as "do not be wordy" only mark one thing to avoid and leave the rest open. Negatives still have a place, especially for hard limits, but they work best when paired with a positive alternative.

This guide explains why, when to use each style and how to rewrite common negatives.

## Why negatives are weaker

A prohibition tells the AI what to steer away from but not where to steer. If you write "do not use jargon," the model must guess what you do want. It might choose very simple language, or a different kind of jargon, or an overly casual tone. A positive instruction collapses the guesswork: "explain every technical term in one short phrase."

There is a second effect. Mentioning a thing, even to forbid it, puts it into the prompt. If you write "do not mention pricing," the topic is now on the page, and the model can sometimes drift toward it. Positive framing keeps attention on what you want.

Results vary by model and task, so treat this as a strong tendency rather than a law, and test with your own prompts.

## Rewriting negatives as positives

Here are common negatives and better versions:

| Negative | Positive rewrite |
| --- | --- |
| Do not be wordy | Use no more than 100 words and one idea per sentence |
| Do not use jargon | Use everyday words; explain any technical term in brackets |
| Don't be too formal | Write like a friendly colleague, using contractions |
| Do not give a long intro | Start with the answer in the first sentence |
| Don't make things up | Use only the text provided; reply "not in the text" if absent |
| Don't use bullet points | Write in two short paragraphs of flowing prose |

The positive forms are also easier to verify, because you can check whether the answer begins with the answer or stays under 100 words.

## When negatives are the right tool

Negative instructions are not forbidden. They are useful when:

- **A limit is absolute.** "Do not include personal data in the output."
- **You are correcting a repeated habit.** "Do not end with a summary paragraph."
- **There is no simple positive.** "Avoid the words 'revolutionary' and 'game-changing'."
- **Safety or honesty matters.** "Do not invent citations."

Even then, add what to do instead. "Do not invent citations; if you cannot name a real source, say so and suggest what type of source I should search for" is far more useful than the prohibition alone.

## A before-and-after example

**Before:**

```
Write a product description for a reusable water bottle. Don't be boring,
don't use cliches, don't make it too long, and don't use exclamation marks.
```

**After:**

```
Write a 60-word product description for a reusable steel water bottle,
aimed at commuters. Open with a concrete everyday scene. Use specific
details (capacity, materials, how it fits a bag) rather than general praise.
Keep the tone calm and confident, with full stops only.
```

The second prompt turns four negatives into one clear picture. It also adds audience and length, so the AI does not need to guess.

## Using a short "avoid" list safely

If you have recurring problems, keep a small "avoid" list at the end of the prompt, below the positive instructions:

```
Style:
- Short sentences, active voice, concrete nouns.
- Open with the main point.

Avoid: stock phrases such as "in today's world" and "unlock your potential".
```

Keep the list short. A long list of banned words pulls attention toward them and can make writing stilted.

## Positive instructions for students

Students often write prompts like "Don't just give me the answer." A stronger version is "Guide me with questions. Ask one question at a time and wait for my reply. Give a hint only if I am stuck for two attempts." This spells out the behaviour you want from a tutor and supports real learning rather than copying.

Another example: instead of "Don't use difficult words," write "Explain at the level of a student in Year 9 and define any new term when it first appears."

## Positive instructions for work and writing

For emails, replace "Don't sound rude" with "Be polite and direct; state the request in the first two sentences and thank the reader at the end." For reports, replace "Don't ramble" with "Use the headings Summary, Findings and Next steps, with no more than three sentences under each."

Notice how each positive form is a small specification. That is the main benefit: it makes your expectations concrete.

## Testing the difference

Run a simple experiment. Take a prompt that has several "don't" lines and run it. Then rewrite each negative as a positive and run it again. Compare the outputs for tone, length and focus. Make a note of which rewrites made the biggest difference, and reuse them in your templates.

## Combining with other techniques

Positive framing fits well with other basics. Pair it with format instructions ("a table with these columns"), with examples ("write in the style of this sample") and with constraints ("under 120 words"). Together these give the AI a rich description of the target, so fewer prohibitions are needed.

## Positive framing for tone and personality

Tone instructions are a place where negatives are especially weak. "Don't sound like a robot" does not describe a voice. Try "Write as a thoughtful teacher talking to one student: warm, specific, and willing to say when something is hard." That sentence can be followed, tested and adjusted. If the first result is too chatty, change one word in the description, such as "warm" to "calm," instead of adding another prohibition.

## Common mistakes

- **Stacking many prohibitions.** Long lists of "don't" clutter the prompt and can backfire.
- **Naming the thing you want to avoid in detail.** Describing the unwanted content can bring it into the answer.
- **Using negatives for style.** "Don't sound robotic" says little; describe the voice you want.
- **Giving contradictory rules.** "Don't be formal" and "use professional language" conflict.
- **Never testing.** Behaviour differs across tools, so check how yours responds.
- **Forgetting honesty rules.** Keep clear limits on invented facts, with a positive fallback.

## Next steps

Rewrite your own instructions in the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), see positively framed examples in the [prompt library](/prompts), or try them on [writing prompts](/prompts/category/writing).

faq.q: Why do 'do not' instructions sometimes fail with AI?
faq.a: Prohibitions mark what to avoid but not what to do, so the model still has to guess. Mentioning the unwanted thing can also bring it into focus. Positive instructions give a clearer target.

faq.q: Should I never use negative instructions in prompts?
faq.a: No. Negatives suit hard limits, repeated bad habits, and safety or honesty rules. Pair them with a positive fallback, such as saying 'not in the text' instead of guessing, so the AI knows what to do.

faq.q: How do I rewrite 'don't be wordy' as a positive?
faq.a: Give a measurable target, such as 'use no more than 100 words, one idea per sentence, and begin with the main point.' Concrete positives are easier for the AI to follow and for you to check.

faq.q: Does this advice work for every AI tool?
faq.a: Behaviour varies between tools and versions, so treat it as a strong tendency. Test your own prompts, compare results with and without negatives, and keep what works for your tasks.

title: Let AI Ask Clarifying Questions Before It Answers You
excerpt: Ask the AI to question you first and your answers get sharper. Learn the interview-style prompt, when to use it and copy-ready templates for study and work.
seo_title: Let AI Ask Clarifying Questions Before It Answers You
seo_description: Learn how to make AI ask clarifying questions before it answers, with interview-style prompt templates for study, writing and planning, plus tips and mistakes.
content:
When your request is complex or you are not sure what to include, tell the AI to ask you questions before it answers. A line such as "Ask me up to five questions you need answered to do this well, then wait for my replies" turns a one-way request into a short interview and usually produces a far more tailored result.

It is one of the simplest techniques in prompting, and it solves a common problem: you do not know what the AI needs, and the AI cannot see what you did not say.

## Why asking questions first works

Most weak answers come from missing information. You could try to predict everything the AI needs and write a very long prompt, but that is hard, especially for unfamiliar tasks. Letting the AI ask questions reverses the burden. The model surfaces the gaps, and you fill them with facts only you know.

It also improves your own thinking. Questions such as "Who is the audience?" and "What would success look like?" often force you to clarify your goals before any text is written.

## The basic pattern

```
I want help with [task].

Before you start, ask me up to [number] questions that would help you give
a specific, useful answer. Ask them in a numbered list. Do not answer yet;
wait for my replies.
```

After you answer, say "Now go ahead," or ask for the output in a particular format. If some questions do not apply, reply "skip" for those.

## Best times to use it

This method is especially helpful when:

- the task is open-ended, such as planning a project or writing a speech
- you are new to a subject and do not know what matters
- the answer depends on your personal situation
- earlier attempts gave generic results
- the stakes are moderate and a better fit saves rework

For quick facts or simple edits it adds unnecessary steps.

## Templates you can copy

### Study plan interview

```
Act as a study coach. I need a revision plan for [exam].
Ask me 5 questions about my timeline, current level, weak topics,
available hours and preferred study methods. Wait for my answers, then
create a week-by-week plan in a table.
```

### Writing brief interview

```
I need to write [type of document]. Interview me to build a brief.
Ask one question at a time, covering audience, purpose, key message,
tone and length. After the last question, summarise the brief in five
bullets and ask whether to start drafting.
```

### Decision helper

```
I am deciding between [options]. Ask me what you need to know about my
priorities, constraints and risks, one question at a time. When you have
enough, give a comparison table and a recommendation, and state your
assumptions.
```

### Career application helper

```
I am applying for [role]. Ask me questions about my relevant experience,
skills and projects, one at a time. Use only what I tell you; do not
invent achievements. Then suggest three resume summary options.
```

## One question or many?

Asking for all questions at once is quick, and you can answer in a single reply. Asking for one question at a time feels more like a conversation and works well for complex or emotional topics, because later questions can depend on earlier answers. Choose based on your task. A limit such as "no more than five questions" prevents a long interrogation.

## How to answer well

Short, factual answers are enough. Number your replies to match the questions. If you do not know, say so: "Not sure; suggest a sensible default." If a question reveals that you have not decided something, take a moment to decide, since that clarity will improve the final result.

## A worked example

**Prompt:**

```
I want to start a small newsletter about local hiking trails. Before giving
advice, ask me up to five questions.
```

**AI questions (summarised):** Who is the audience? How often will you publish? What is your experience level with writing? Do you want to earn money? What tools do you already use?

**Your reply:**

```
1. Local hikers aged 25-45. 2. Twice a month. 3. Beginner. 4. Not at first.
5. Only email and a phone camera.
```

**Next prompt:** "Now give me a six-week launch plan and three example issue outlines." The plan now fits your real situation rather than being a generic list.

## Combining with other techniques

You can ask the AI to restate the brief at the end: "Summarise what you understood in four bullets so I can correct anything." This catches misunderstandings early. You can also add constraints before the interview, such as "Keep the final answer under 300 words," and let the questions fill in the rest.

## Limits to remember

The AI's questions may be generic or miss something important, so add your own context when you notice a gap. Questions do not guarantee accuracy of the final answer, so still verify facts. And do not share sensitive personal details just because a question asks; answer in general terms or skip.

## Asking the AI to explain its questions

If a question puzzles you, ask why it matters. "Why do you need to know my deadline?" often reveals how the AI will use the answer, which teaches you about the task itself. For instance, a study coach may explain that the deadline determines how much time to give to review versus new material. You can then decide whether you want that trade-off, which makes you a more active participant instead of a passive recipient of a plan.

## Reusing a good interview

If an interview produces an excellent result, save the questions and your answers. Next time you can paste your earlier answers, update the parts that changed and skip the interview. Over time you will build a small profile of your preferences, such as reading level, usual time available and favourite formats, that you can include in future prompts or standing instructions.

## Common mistakes

- **Not limiting the number of questions.** You may get a long list that feels like a form.
- **Forgetting to say "wait for my reply."** The AI may ask questions and answer anyway.
- **Giving vague replies.** "Whatever" gives the model nothing to work with.
- **Using it for trivial tasks.** A simple request does not need an interview.
- **Skipping the summary check.** Confirm understanding before the final output.
- **Over-sharing private details.** Keep answers relevant and safe.

faq.q: When should I use clarifying questions in a prompt?
faq.a: Use them for open-ended or personal tasks such as planning, writing briefs or decisions, and when earlier answers felt generic. Skip them for quick facts or small edits where they only add steps.

faq.a: All at once is faster; one at a time suits complex topics because later questions can build on earlier answers. Set a maximum number of questions so the process stays short.
